summary:
Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct. Both male and female same-sex activity has been lawful since 1975, and the age of consent is 14 irrespective of sexual orientation or gender. The sources record no anti-trans statute, no arrest pattern and no police targeting of transgender people, and no law barring trans people from public facilities, health care or employment.

No legal gender recognition procedure is documented in the sources reviewed. The operative document for a trans visitor is the passport or identity card issued at home, including any marker changed there; there is no domestic route to alter or regularise a marker while in the country.

Health policy is required to be non-discriminatory on gender identity grounds. Law No. 13/2022, the second amendment to the Health System Law, provides at Article 3-2(o) that health policy must ensure access to family planning, reproductive, school, visual, oral and mental health care and early diagnosis without discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Reported practice diverges: LGBTI people are described as often verbally abused and discriminated against in some public services, medical centres among them.

Protection instruments issued in 2024 name transgender people explicitly. Ministerial Decree No. 11/MSSI/V/2024 requires children and young people, regardless of gender, nationality, sexual orientation, religion or disability, to have adequate access to protection services and protection from sexual and gender-based violence, abuse and exploitation; its standard operating procedure defines non-binary gender identity, includes transgender children within its definition of LGBTI children, states that transgender children may be at greater risk of prejudice, stigma, violence or difficulty accessing humanitarian services, and requires case managers to respond to needs on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation. Ministerial Decree No. 10/MSSI/V/2024 on gender-based violence extends protection expressly to lesbian, bisexual, transgender and intersex people, bars social workers from discriminating on grounds of gender or sexual orientation, and prohibits revealing a person's gender identity or sexual orientation without authorisation. Law No. 6/2023, Article 6(n), gives children and young people equal rights and prohibits discrimination based on sex, gender and sexual orientation.

Hate-crime and non-discrimination law covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. Bias based on sexual orientation has been an aggravating circumstance for crimes since 2009. There is no general anti-discrimination law on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; a clause barring discrimination on sexual orientation was removed from the draft Constitution by 52 votes of 88 before the Constitution took effect in 2002. Sectoral provisions reach sexual orientation only: Article 3(3) of the Penal Execution Regime Decree-Law No. 14/2014 requires imprisonment to be executed impartially without discrimination based on sexual orientation, Article 2(i) of the Land Law No. 13/2017 lists sexual orientation among vulnerable groups, and Article 3 of the trafficking law No. 3/2017 requires victim protection without discrimination on that ground.

Police conduct rules follow the same pattern. Decree-Law No. 44/2020, Article 13(1), requires respectful treatment without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Decree-Law No. 69/2022, Articles 15(6)(f) and 18(b), bans such discrimination; and Decree-Law No. 35/2024, Articles 16(f) and 17(b), requires missions and action without hindrance or discrimination by reason of sexual orientation. Physical abuse in public or by public authorities is described as uncommon, but no source documents enforcement of these provisions in a case involving a transgender person.

Partnership recognition is closed. Article 1467 of the Civil Code, Law No. 10/2011, defines marriage as a contract between two people of different sex, and Article 1517 declares a marriage contracted by two people of the same sex legally non-existent. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no spousal recognition, and no source indicates that such a partner can obtain residence, next-of-kin standing or medical decision-making authority on that basis. Protection may still be available: the Domestic Violence Law No. 07/2010 treats people who live or have lived in conditions analogous to spouses as family, without requiring cohabitation, and covers intimate relationships regardless of gender.

Violence against transgender people is documented as family and community-based rather than state-directed. CODIVA records that transgender members of the community are particularly vulnerable to harassment and discrimination, and that transgender students are more likely to be bullied and to drop out at secondary level. A November study for Rede Feto with lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men in Dili and Bobonaro documented corrective rape, physical and psychological abuse, ostracism, discrimination and marginalisation by family members. A 2017 survey of 57 young lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men found that 86 per cent had experienced physical and psychological violence, including domestic violence, forced marriages and attempts by family members to change their sexual orientation or gender identity; the sample is small and self-selected, so the figure describes that group rather than a population rate.

Senior officials have publicly endorsed the annual Pride march. The first parade, in 2017, drew a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister. A second parade was held in Dili on 20 July 2018, and the third, on 12 July 2019, drew an estimated 3,000 participants, six times the 2017 turnout, with President Francisco Guterres stating "I am a President for all people". Reporting on the same period records day-to-day rejection, including hostile messages sent to the family of the 2017 organiser.

A 2017 report by the US State Department recorded that same-sex conduct was not criminalised but that the law provided no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, that transgender people remained particularly vulnerable to societal discrimination, stigma and violence limiting access to employment, education and health care, and that no government action had been taken to prevent discrimination or violence.
tangentialFactors:
Timor-Leste's diplomatic record on sexual orientation and gender identity is supportive but thin. It is recorded in favour of the 2011 UN Human Rights Council joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity and of a 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability and disability; neither creates a domestic obligation a visitor can invoke.

The Defence Force decrees (Decree-Law No. 17/2006, No. 33/2020, No. 3/2021 and No. 5/2022) contain no explicit bar on LGBTQ people serving and no inclusive anti-discrimination measure either. The Constitution and statute are silent on same-sex relations.

Detention conditions are governed by the same sexual-orientation-only formula as other sectoral rules, so a trans person held in custody has no gender-identity-specific safeguard on the face of the Penal Execution Regime Decree-Law.
localsOnly:
Residents face the gaps a visitor only brushes. No specific employment protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity exists, and access to education is limited for LGBTI people who have been removed from the family home or who fear abuse at school; transgender students are recorded as more likely to be bullied and to leave secondary school.

The 2024 child-protection standard operating procedure binds case managers to respond to the needs of transgender children on the basis of gender identity, and the gender-based violence decree binds social workers to use non-critical language, to set aside preconceptions and to keep a person's gender identity or sexual orientation confidential without authorisation.

Land Law No. 13/2017 lists sexual orientation among vulnerable groups for the purposes of land administration, and the trafficking law requires victim protection without discrimination on that ground.

Military service is not closed by any of the Defence Force decrees, but none of them provides an inclusive anti-discrimination guarantee.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any administrative gender-recognition route exists outside published law is unresolved; the sources describe none.

No source describes airport or security screening practice for trans travellers, document-marker flagging at the border, or the treatment of a passport marker that differs from a traveller's presentation.

No trans-specific hate-crime statistics are published, and the enforcement record of the police non-discrimination decrees in cases involving transgender people is not sourced.

The 86 per cent violence figure derives from a 57-person survey sample and is not a population rate; no general-population comparison appears in the sources.

Whether a foreign partner in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status can obtain any residence or next-of-kin recognition is not addressed by any source.
